title: First Aid & Safety · Episode 4
chapters: Floods: if it's flooded, forget it
Home fires: alarms, escape plans and kitchen fires

units.t: First Aid & Safety. Episode four.
In this episode: Floods: if it's flooded, forget it, Severe storms and cyclones and Home fires: alarms, escape plans and kitchen fires.
Part one. Floods: if it's flooded, forget it.
Floodwater that looks shallow and calm can sweep a car off the road in seconds.
Here is how floods catch people out, and how to stay on the right side of the water.
Never drive through.
Picture a country road after heavy rain, brown water covering a dip for twenty metres.
You know this road, and it looks barely ankle-deep.
But floodwater is murky.
You can't see how deep it is, whether the road has washed away, or what lies beneath.
Driving into floodwater is one of the most common ways people die in Australian floods, which is why emergency services say: if it's flooded, forget it.
A car is a sealed box of air.
In a few tens of centimetres of water it starts to float and the tyres lose grip, so a current can sweep it away.
Fast-flowing water around knee height can knock an adult off their feet.
Never drive, walk, ride or swim through floodwater.
Know your flood risk.
Australia's rivers can rise slowly over days or explode in minutes.
Riverine floods build as rain upstream drains into big catchments, giving hours or days of warning.
Flash floods follow intense downpours, often in hilly or built-up areas, where drains overflow and creeks rise almost instantly.
Storm surge from cyclones can flood low-lying coastal land.
Find out whether your home, work or regular routes are at risk.
Many councils publish flood maps, and state emergency service websites explain local risks.
Notice small clues too: a street called Creek Road, a low dip on the way to school, or a causeway with depth markers.
Trust those markers.
Warnings and preparing.

The Australian Warning System has three levels: Advice, an incident has started, stay up to date, Watch and Act, conditions are changing, act now, and Emergency Warning, you are in danger, act immediately.
The Bureau of Meteorology issues flood watches and warnings.
Check your state emergency service website and app, the Bureau, and local ABC radio.
Don't wait for a warning if water is rising around you.
The best time to prepare is on a sunny day.
Plan where you would go and how, without crossing flooded roads.
Pack a kit with a torch, battery radio, medicines, document copies, chargers and water.
Plan early for pets and livestock.
Store valuables up high, and check what your insurance covers, because flood cover is not automatic.
For non-life-threatening help, call the SES on 132 500.
When the water rises.
If authorities tell you to evacuate, go, and go early.
Roads can be cut long before water reaches your door, and leaving late often means crossing rising water in the dark.
If you are trapped and your life is in danger, call Triple Zero, 000.
Move to the highest safe point of the building with a phone, torch and warm clothes, and wait for rescue rather than trying to swim out.
Never let children play in floodwater or stormwater drains, which can suck people in.
Floodwater can carry sewage, chemicals, sharp debris and displaced snakes and spiders, so avoid touching it and wash well if you do.
This is general information; follow your state emergency service's advice.
After the flood.
When floodwater recedes, new hazards appear.
Only return home when authorities say it is safe.
Power lines may be down, and any appliance or wiring that has been underwater should be checked by a licensed electrician before use.
If you smell gas, leave and call for help.
Walls and floors may be weakened, and mud can hide broken glass, nails and animals.
Wear gloves, sturdy boots and long sleeves while cleaning, and wash your hands often.
Throw out any food that touched floodwater, and check with your council or water authority before drinking tap water.
Floods are emotionally exhausting, so check on neighbours and ask for help yourself.
The key idea: If it's flooded, forget it: floodwater hides depth, damage and current, and cars and people are easily swept away.
Part two. Severe storms and cyclones.
Every year, wild storms and tropical cyclones tear roofs off, drop trees on cars and cut power to thousands of homes.
Knowing what to do before and during one can keep your family safe.
Storm country.
On a hot spring afternoon in south-east Queensland or western Sydney, towering clouds can drop giant hail, flatten fences and flood streets in under an hour.
Severe thunderstorms happen across most of Australia.
In the tropical north the bigger threat is the tropical cyclone, which forms over warm ocean water.
The cyclone season runs from November to April.
The Bureau of Meteorology rates cyclones from Category 1 to 5, with Category 3 and above called severe.
But the category describes only wind.
A weaker cyclone can still be deadly through flooding rain, which can spread hundreds of kilometres inland, or storm surge.
Cyclones can also strengthen rapidly or change direction, so don't relax at 'only' a low category.
The danger of storm surge.
When a strong cyclone nears a coast, powerful winds push ocean water toward the shore, and the low air pressure at its centre lets the sea bulge upward.
The result is a storm surge: sea level well above normal high tide, topped with large waves.
If it arrives at high tide, it can flood low-lying coastal suburbs, roads and caravan parks.
Around the world, surge has caused many of the deadliest cyclone disasters.
In Australia, authorities may order people in surge zones to evacuate even if their homes are well built, because the threat is water, not wind.
If you live near the coast in cyclone country, find out whether you are in a storm surge zone.
Preparing your home.
Much storm damage comes from flying debris and falling trees.
Before the season, clean gutters and downpipes, trim overhanging branches, use a qualified arborist for large trees, and check the roof.
List loose items such as trampolines, outdoor furniture, bins and pot plants to secure or bring inside when a warning is issued.
In cyclone areas, residents often fit shutters or protect windows, and learn whether their home was built to modern cyclone standards.
Keep your emergency kit stocked, fill vehicles with fuel, and charge phones and power banks when a warning comes.
Park cars under cover or away from trees if hail is forecast.
For storm damage that is not life-threatening, call the SES on 132 500.
Sheltering safely.
In a severe storm or cyclone, the safest place is usually indoors in the strongest part of the building, often a small internal room such as a bathroom, laundry or hallway, away from windows.
If the building breaks up, protect yourself under a sturdy table or mattress.
In a cyclone, be wary of the calm eye: the wind drops and the sky may clear, then the winds return, often from the opposite direction and just as strong.
Stay in until authorities say it has passed.
Lightning can strike many kilometres from the rain, so if you can hear thunder, you are in range.
Go indoors or into a hard-topped car, and avoid open ground, water and isolated trees.
It is safe to touch a lightning victim; call 000 and start CPR if they aren't breathing normally.
After the storm.
The clean-up brings its own risks.
Always assume fallen power lines are live.
Stay well clear, at least 8 metres according to many electricity networks, and remember that water, fences and wet ground near a line can be electrified too.
Report them to your electricity distributor, or call Triple Zero, 000, if there is immediate danger.
Don't enter badly damaged buildings, and watch for broken glass, exposed nails and asbestos in older homes.
Avoid driving through floodwater or under damaged trees.
Chainsaw and ladder injuries are common after storms, so be cautious or leave big jobs to professionals and the SES.
Photograph damage before clearing it, for insurance.
This is general information; follow official advice for your area.
The key idea: Australia faces severe thunderstorms and tropical cyclones, and cyclone categories describe wind only, not total danger.
Part three. Home fires: alarms, escape plans and kitchen fires.
A house fire can make a home deadly in a matter of minutes.
A working smoke alarm and a practised escape plan are the two things most likely to get everyone out alive.
Minutes, not hours.
Real house fires are not like films.
Modern homes are full of synthetic materials such as foam couches, plastics and carpets that burn hot and fast and release thick, toxic smoke.
A room can become deadly within a few minutes.
Smoke, not flames, is usually what kills, filling the air with poisonous gases like carbon monoxide and blocking your sight.
Many fatal fires happen at night.
You can't rely on smelling smoke to wake you.
Australian states and territories require smoke alarms, but rules differ.
In Queensland, from 1 January 2027 every home must have interconnected photoelectric alarms in each bedroom, hallway and level.
Test monthly, clean vents, and replace alarms about ten years old.
Check your state fire service website.
Escape plan and exit.
At 2 am you won't have time to think.
Draw a floor plan and mark two ways out of each room, usually a door and a window.
Make sure security screens and deadlocks open quickly from inside.
Choose a meeting place outside, such as the letterbox.
Practise with everyone, including children, once or twice a year, and teach children to get out, not hide under beds.
In smoke, get low and crawl to the nearest safe exit.
Feel a closed door with the back of your hand; if hot, use another way.
Close doors behind you.
Once out, call 000 and stay out.
Never go back for pets or belongings.
If clothes catch fire: stop, drop, cover your face and roll.
Kitchen fires.
The kitchen is where many house fires start, often when someone leaves food cooking and gets distracted.
Fire services say it neatly: keep looking while cooking.
If a pan of oil or fat catches fire, never throw water on it.
Water sinks under the hot oil, flashes into steam and can blast burning oil across the kitchen.
Instead, if it is safe, turn off the heat and smother the flames by sliding a lid or fire blanket over the pan, then leave it covered until completely cool.
Don't carry the burning pan outside.
A fire blanket near the kitchen exit is cheap and easy to use.
If the fire is spreading or you're unsure, get everyone out, close the door and call Triple Zero, 000.
Heaters, power, batteries.
Winter brings more house fires as heaters, electric blankets and dryers work harder.
Keep heaters at least a metre from curtains, bedding, clothes and furniture, and turn them off when you leave the room or go to bed.
Check electric blankets for frayed cords before winter.
Clean the dryer lint filter every use.
Avoid overloading power boards, and never cover them with rugs.
A newer worry is lithium-ion batteries in e-bikes, e-scooters and power tools.
Damaged or poor-quality batteries can overheat and burn fiercely.
Use the supplied charger, avoid charging bulky batteries overnight or near your exit path, and stop using any battery that is swollen, hot or damaged.
Burns first aid.
If someone is burned, Australian first aid advice is clear: cool the burn under cool running water for 20 minutes.
This helps even if some time has passed.
Remove jewellery and clothing from the area unless stuck to the skin.
Do not use ice, butter, toothpaste or creams.
After cooling, cover the burn loosely with plastic cling wrap or a clean non-stick dressing, and keep the person warm.
Call Triple Zero, 000, for burns that are large, deep, on the face, hands, feet, groin or airway, caused by chemicals or electricity, or on a child or older person.
This is general information only.
A proper first aid course teaches these skills hands-on and is one of the best investments a household can make.
The key idea: Smoke is what kills in house fires, so a working smoke alarm giving early warning is vital.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is driving through floodwater so dangerous?
Answer. Hidden depth and damage, and cars can float.
Question two. What does a cyclone's category describe?
Answer. Wind strength only.
Question three. What usually kills people in house fires?
Answer. Smoke and poisonous gases.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
